one_liner: Small table-driven C x86/x86-64 decoder; in decode-only mode it beat Zydis, bddisasm and XED, but it formats slowest.
what_it_does: libudis86 decodes a stream of x86 or x86-64 bytes into a flat ud_t structure (mnemonic, prefixes, up to four explicit operands) and can optionally render Intel (NASM) or AT&T syntax. The API is a C state object: ud_init, ud_set_mode, ud_set_input_buffer (or a FILE* or callback hook), then a ud_decode or ud_disassemble loop; udcli is a small command-line front end. It is not a drop-in for Zydis, XED or Capstone: the API, operand model and mnemonic enums all differ.
how_it_is_fast: Decoding is a walk over generated lookup tables. scripts/ud_itab.py compiles docs/x86/optable.xml into itab.c, and decode_ext() follows table pointers keyed by opcode byte, mod, reg, rm, mode, operand size, SSE prefix and VEX.L/W until it reaches an instruction entry. Per-instruction work is small: one ud_t reused across calls, no dynamic allocation, only explicit operands decoded, and no flags, implicit-operand or CPUID metadata. Formatting is a separate pass (the translator pointer runs only in ud_disassemble) built on vsnprintf, which is why decode+format is slow.
when_to_use: Quick length decoding or mnemonic and operand inspection of SSE-era x86-64 code (up to SSE4.2, AES and AVX1) in a C or C++ tool where a BSD-2 licence and a single small library matter.
Maintaining an existing tool that already uses the udis86 API, where porting would cost more than the ISA gaps.
Decode-only scans (instruction boundaries and opcode classes) where 80.72 MB/s on a 2021 Skylake was enough and you never print the text.
when_not_to_use: Modern compiler output: the opcode table has no AVX2 (vpbroadcast*, vpermd, vinserti128, gathers), FMA3 (vfmadd*), BMI1/BMI2 (bextr, pdep, shlx, tzcnt), LZCNT, F16C, ADX or EVEX/AVX-512 entries, so those bytes decode as invalid.
Producing text: at 12.02 MB/s decode+format it was the slowest of nine libraries, behind Capstone (14.02 MB/s) and far behind Zydis (22.24), diStorm (58.85) and iced (149.21).

Anything that needs accuracy guarantees or security hardening. There have been no commits since Dec 2014; 48 issues are open, among them wrong-decoding reports #129 (operand size), #126 (truncated jump target with 0x66), #107 (rdtscp on Intel) and #101 (popfw in 64-bit mode), plus 22 unmerged PRs; there is no fuzzing (OSS-Fuzz request #130 is open).
When raw decode speed is the goal: in the same harness iced (256.69 MB/s), yaxpeax-x86 (182.08) and diStorm (92.17) decoded faster.

integration.dependencies: none at run time; Python is needed at build time to generate itab.c and itab.h from optable.xml, and autotools for the Unix build (a VS2010 project is included)
integration.min_toolchain: C89-era C compiler with autoconf/automake/libtool. Python 3 builds need the ud_opcode.py fix that disas-bench applies with sed (issues #120, #123).
integration.platforms: any host that compiles C; decodes 16-, 32- and 64-bit x86 code
integration.thread_safety: Re-entrant per the README: all state lives in the caller's ud_t, so use one ud_t per thread.

gotchas: The decode-only rows are not like for like. The bddisasm harness skips 1 byte after a failed decode, while udis86 consumes every byte it has read so far and marks them invalid. No row counts invalid instructions or checks that the libraries walked xul.dll the same way, so the AVX2, FMA and BMI bytes udis86 cannot decode can change its path through the file. udis86's ud_decode also returns less per instruction (explicit operands only) than full-mode decoders. Against Zydis in its minimal mode (Zydis (min), 61.33 MB/s) the lead shrinks to about 1.32x (derived from page data), compared with 2.36x against default Zydis.

Build handicap, not an advantage: make-all.sh runs udis86's ./configure with no CFLAGS, so the library gets the autoconf default -g -O2 without LTO. The other C libraries were built with -flto (XED with --opt=3, Capstone and bddisasm as CMake Release). Each library ran once (bench.py, clock() CPU time, MB meaning MiB).

The record's ISA note needs a correction. master's docs/x86/optable.xml does contain VEX and AVX1 forms (SSE entries tagged 'sse avx', vbroadcastss, vinsertf128, vperm2f128, vzeroupper, vtestps); it lacks AVX2, FMA, BMI and AVX-512, although the README lists extensions only up to SSE4.2/AES.

Building is fragile on current toolchains: the generated itab order varies between Python versions (#144), and autoconf and Arch Linux build errors are open (#142, #146). The uninitialised curr reported in decode_prefixes against 1.7.2 (#116) is initialised on master, so build from master, not the 1.7.2 tarball.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Rarely. diStorm3 is also plain C and beat udis86 in both modes of the same harness (92.17 against 80.72 MB/s decode, 58.85 against 12.02 MB/s decode+format), and Zydis, bddisasm or XED give full modern ISA coverage. Keep udis86 only for an existing integration or a tiny SSE-era decoder with a BSD-2 licence.
verified_claims_summary: The measurement is icedland/disas-bench (2021, Kubuntu 21.04, gcc 10.3.0, i5-6600K), one run per library over the 77 MB .text of Firefox 86.0.1 xul.dll. It recorded udis86 at 80.72 MB/s decode-only, against Zydis 34.19, bddisasm 35.48 and XED 55.39 MB/s (about 2.36x, 2.28x and 1.46x, derived from page data), with udis86 built at -O2 without LTO. In decode+format udis86 was last at 12.02 MB/s, below Capstone's 14.02. Upstream athre0z/disas-bench later dropped udis86, so no newer run exists.
status_note: Abandoned since Dec 2014 (293 commits, 1.1k stars, 319 forks, BSD-2-Clause), with no AVX2 or AVX-512 coverage. It is copyable and small, but suits only legacy integrations. A 2025 community fork (MIvanchev/udis86, issue #147) is two commits ahead and announces no ISA work.
